prompt: There is a speech-sound disorder, not caused by a structural abnormality, for which one symptom is rearranging sounds of a word. The term for the disorder was first defined in 1908 by a German neuroscientist with the first name Hugo. Why was the Nobel Peace Prize given to an American the same year Hugo died?
answer:
The premise contains a factual mix-up.

The disorder is **apraxia of speech**. Its terminology is associated with the German neurologist **Hugo Liepmann**, who died on **May 6, 1925**. However, the **1925 Nobel Peace Prize was not awarded to an American**: it went to **Sir Austen Chamberlain**, a British statesman, for his role in the **Locarno Treaties**, which aimed to stabilize post–World War I Europe.

The likely source of the confusion is **Charles G. Dawes**, an American who received the **1925 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences**—not the Peace Prize—for his work on the **Dawes Plan**, which addressed Germany’s postwar reparations and helped promote European financial and political stability.
